dispositions.method: The automatic families first printed in 1777 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 341 items printed somewhere), and the families of 1776 were looked for on the 1777 pages (items_from_1776.json: 39 items). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page (about 220 words of its text, both transcriptions); every page was swept for seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers; every candidate was counted by its own opening over all 1,320 pages in both transcriptions and the matches were read; every admitted story and every candidate set aside was searched with phrase searches (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).
dispositions.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (register Y-THIN) as amended by the owner's choice B1 on 23 November 2026: an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4; digests are not. As in R-01, items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35, a target, not a quota); one affair's items as in X-1800-01. The eligible items not chosen are listed with their counts and are not checked against the scans. Sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) apply as in every year.
dispositions.paper_counting: 1777 has 11 catalogue series, which are 10 papers: Dunlap's Pennsylvania Packet (Philadelphia, to 9 September) and The Pennsylvania Packet (Lancaster, from 29 November) are one paper (C-04). The Newport Gazette and the New-York Gazette were printed in towns the British held. The release's map lists two misfiled RevX pages for 1777 (the Freeman's Journal of 8 March, pages 2 and 3); no 1777 issue has a corrected date.

items_admitted.boston-report-privateer-takes-six-prizes: the sweep of passages shared word for word by 4 or more papers

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted item by item over all 1,320 pages, 91 items met the bar in the count of 23 November. The reading and the phrase searches left 88 eligible items (86 groups, and two reports of an affair already chosen), and the sweep checked again on 24 November added 9 (X-1777-08), 97 in all: three items fell below the bar by their own words (the brig Warren, the London paragraph on the high treason bill, Captain Fisk's prize), one letter is merged with the letter it sends, and Sir Joseph Yorke's memorial reaches the bar with its two translations counted together. One item is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks and is admitted: the articles of convention of Saratoga (7 of 7). Of the others, 35 are chosen (26 stories, 36 groups, 186 printings), 60 are listed as eligible and not chosen, and one that turns on a private person is listed for the owner.
counted_item_by_item.The bar: Y-THIN: more than half of the papers that survive for the item's weeks (a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and at least 4. 1777 has 10 papers; 5 to 9 are in print in an item's weeks, so the bar is 4 for most items and 5 where the weeks reach late April to early June, when the two Charleston papers survive.
counted_item_by_item.Letters printed together: A letter and the copy it sends are one item, counted by the first that stands on the page (X-1810-01): General Washington's letter to Congress of 25 July with his letter to General Howe of 16 July; General Gates's letter of 20 October with his letter to General Vaughan; Lord Cornwallis's letter with Lieutenant Colonel Walcott's demand. The separate letters of a correspondence are counted one by one (the exchange of prisoners; General Gates and General Burgoyne).
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: C-02: the Baltimore report of a French fleet at Charleston in two forms (3 + 2 papers), Sir Joseph Yorke's memorial in two translations (2 + 2) and the Philadelphia paragraph on prisoners and deserters after the landing at Elk in two forms (3 + 1). Each reaches the bar only together (Q-04).
counted_item_by_item.Pages that reword, summarise or recite a: Not counted (C-07): Purdie's summary of the April letters on the exchange of prisoners; Dixon and Hunter's paraphrase of General Washington's proclamation of 25 January; a Baltimore paragraph about Governor Henry's proclamation; the state proclamations that recite Congress's resolution for a thanksgiving; a Loan Office notice in Purdie's Virginia Gazette (10 and 31 October, 14 November) that restates Congress's resolution of 10 September on the interest of loan office certificates.
counted_item_by_item.Pages first counted for another text: Read and taken out: two pages with Congress's thanks to Colonel Greene (not the thanks to Lieutenant Colonels Meigs and Barton); two pages with an answer headed 'To John Burgoyne' (not General Burgoyne's proclamation); the Pennsylvania Packet's page of the messages that passed before the convention of Saratoga; a page with a different letter from Moses Creek of the same date.
counted_item_by_item.Not items of their own: Congress's order of 16 June to publish the letters on the exchange of prisoners (the heading of that publication); a sentence on the King of Prussia's ports inside different letters; the last sentence of the Albany letter of 11 August, which two papers print as a paragraph of its own.

for_user_decision.The papers in print and the bar (X-1777-: As built: Y-THIN as amended (B1), with 10 papers (11 catalogue series) and 5 to 9 papers in print in an item's weeks; the bar (4 for most items, 5 where the weeks reach late April to early June) makes 97 items eligible. The articles of convention of Saratoga, printed by all 7 papers in print, are admitted; 35 others are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news (26 stories in all); 60 eligible items are listed as not chosen and one, turning on a private person, for the owner.
for_user_decision.Choosing among the eligible items (X-177: As built: as X-1800-01 and the standard years' chosen band, the most widely printed items of each month and kind are chosen; of an affair in the same weeks, the most widely printed item, with the separate public acts printed as widely beside it (a letter and its answer, a speech and the address to it, the convention and the letter on it). Not chosen as items of an affair already chosen: General Washington's letter of 20 June, General Schuyler's letter of 7 July, General St. Clair's letter to the printer on General Schuyler, a letter from headquarters on the papers' 'prejudice' toward General St. Clair, General Washington's letter to Congress of 16 July, the Baltimore paragraph on the Eastern Shore rising and the Providence account of General Prescott's capture. Every month from January to November has a story; no eligible item was first printed in December.
for_user_decision.Printed forms counted together (X-1777-0: As built (C-02): three items reach the bar only with their two printed forms counted together (the Baltimore report of a French fleet, 3 + 2, chosen; Sir Joseph Yorke's memorial, 2 + 2, and the Philadelphia paragraph on deserters after the landing at Elk, 3 + 1, eligible and not chosen). Counted apart, none would be eligible (Q-04).
for_user_decision.Names in the letters from Moses Creek an: As built (C-12): the letter of 26 July from Moses Creek tells of a skirmish at Fort Edward and of a young woman taken from a house and killed; the excerpts end before her name and the description does not give it. Her death was much reported in 1777; the owner may prefer her name shown, as the papers print it. The letter from Pittsburgh of 24 March names the man who returned from the Indian country with the news; the excerpts keep his name, as shipmasters named as sources of news are kept (C-12), and end before the names of settlers killed; the owner may prefer his name cut.
for_user_decision.Papers printed under the British (X-1777: As built (R-02): the New-York Gazette and the Newport Gazette, printed in towns the British held, are counted like the other papers; their headings and comments on American texts are described as theirs, as Purdie's heading of the King's speech is described as his.
for_user_decision.Paragraphs of runs of news, a notice and: As built: single paragraphs of runs of London and foreign news are eligible as items (C-09); one is chosen (London, 17 February, on the preparations for the campaign, the only eligible item first printed in May), the eight others are not. The American Crisis is chosen as a published essay (C-10); the lottery's scheme, a notice, is not chosen.
